summary: We are returning to our old friend, our first friend in SSR, the regression module. In block 3 we're not going to be looking at categorical predictors, but at continuous predictors, so the theme of block 3 is life is also continuous.

We are still in the business of trying to predict an outcome variable as best as possible by looking at one or more predictor variables. With continuous predictors, every continuous predictor gets a single regression weight.
These scatter plots between prediction and outcome visualize exactly the proportion of explained variance, which we denote with r-squared. The higher the r-squared, the better the model predicted.

Always plot your data, because plots are a great way already to assess various assumptions. We predict how well an album sells from two predictor variables, advertisement budget and airplay, and a matrix scatter plot gives a first idea of how they are associated.

The explained variance is an effect size, a proportion between zero and one. An F statistic is a test statistic for hypothesis testing, and you can turn your R-squared into an F statistic to test whether the increase in explained variance is significant.

The moment your predictors are associated, the unique contribution of a predictor is harder to quantify. Now we incorporate both advertisement budget and airplay in predicting album sales, and we can even include the interaction effect.

Just as with regression with a single predictor, we can still test whether the regression coefficients are equal to 0 or not. If a coefficient equals 0, it has no predictive value for predicting the outcome variable.

We are still working with the linear model, and if its assumptions are violated, you cannot rely so much anymore on your inferential statistics. Homoscedasticity, the regression equivalent of equal variances, becomes more and more important as you add more predictors to your model.

Multicollinearity means very strongly associated predictor variables, and if all your predictors look the same, you cannot attribute the explained variance to one specific variable anymore. You assess it with the VIF, and only for the main effects, not for the interaction effect.

chapter: The bootstrap as a robust alternative
summary: If you have one of these assumption problems, you can also choose to use what's called the bootstrap. It is a way to have more robust confidence intervals when you have such assumption violations.
The actual example predicts album sales from two predictor variables, airplay and advertisement budget. We have 200 observations, so the normality assumption is not going to be so important anymore.

chapter: From a regression line to a regression plane
summary: With one predictor, a line gives the predictions of the model. With two predictors, we visualize our model predictions with a plane, chosen in such a way that it's as close to all the points as possible.

Based on the regression weights, we can calculate the predictions that our model makes. You can also plug new values of airplay and advertisement budget into the regression formula to make predictions for new data.

We take the difference between observed and predicted, and that is our model error, our model residuals. R-squared is the squared correlation between observed and predicted, but you can also see it as the model sums of squares divided by the total sums of squares.

Hierarchical regression allows you to get a better idea of an individual predictor's contribution, where the next model builds upon the previous one. We look at the R-squared change, and this R-squared change also has a corresponding F statistic that you can use to do hypothesis testing.

The model summary table tells something about each model as a whole, and the coefficients table lists the regression coefficients corresponding to each predictor. On open questions, always be more specific about what p-value you refer to.

For influential cases you tick Case-wise diagnostics, and a Cook's distance close to one tells you that you have an influential case. The residuals versus predicted plot assesses homoscedasticity, and the tolerance and VIF box checks multicollinearity.

In the Model tab we make multiple models, and we control for a variable by adding it to all the models. Adding airplay gives a significant increase in R-squared, but adding the interaction effect gives barely any increase.

We've seen how to say something about overall model performance with the r-squared, and how to make more specific model comparisons where the only difference between two models is a single predictor. Tomorrow is mediation analysis, explicitly modeling dependence between predictors.

Today is all about an analysis called mediation analysis, and we're also going to be discovering a new JASP module, the Process module. A mediator comes in between two entities, so we see whether the association between two variables is mediated by a third variable.

chapter: Multiple regression as a path model (applet)
summary: We can visualize our regression model with a path model, with boxes for the predictors and a box for the outcome, connected with a regular line. Multiple regression is just based on correlations, and a causal interpretation needs to stem from your methodology, where you experimentally manipulate your predictor variable.

You start with an association between two variables, and then you ask to what extent this relationship is mediated by a third variable. The predictor can directly influence the outcome (the direct relationship), or influence the mediator, which then influences the outcome (the indirect relationship).

As in ANCOVA and partial correlations, this is about the overlap between what your predictor variables explain. The overlap between all three variables (box C) is the indirect effect, and mediation separates it from the direct contribution of the predictor (box A).

The example is about how likely people are to buy sugar after reading an article about an incoming sugar crisis, placed either on the front page or somewhere in the middle. We ask whether the association between condition and intention is mediated by perceived media influence, how much people think other people will buy sugar after that article.

The total effect is the simple relationship between our one predictor, condition, and our one outcome variable, intention. We are not yet dissecting it into indirect and direct effect, and we could test it with a linear regression (or an ANOVA).

To get an idea of the indirect effect, we also look at the regression of our mediator, media influence, on our predictor, condition. The combined effect models the outcome from the predictor and the mediator at the same time, so that is a multiple regression.

chapter: The data and the three regression models
summary: We run a series of regressions that reflect the extent to which the predictor is associated with the outcome, but also with the mediator. If your predictor and your mediator are completely uncorrelated, then you will not have any indirect effect.

chapter: Path plot and the indirect effect
summary: Based on those regression coefficients, we can fill in our path diagram of mediation. The indirect effect is the product of the a and b pathways, and if we add the indirect effect to the direct effect, we get back the total effect.

The most important effect size is just the indirect effect, reported with a p-value, or a confidence interval if you are more interested in estimating it. To test for mediation, we test the indirect effect a × b itself.

The one thing to take away in terms of assumptions for mediation, but also moderation, is the bootstrap. It is a robust tool to get confidence intervals that do not rely on the normality and homoscedasticity assumptions.

The p-value of the indirect effect answers how likely it is to observe this estimate, or more extreme, if on the population level there is no mediation effect. Now that we have multiple p-values in our output, always be specific about which p-value you are referring to.

Process models answer causal questions, but they are very, very often misused (Julia Rohrer's 2022 paper outlines the pitfalls). If you simply throw observational data into a process model you get all sorts of estimates, but numbers alone don't give you enough ground to make causal claims.

With observational data on three variables, we cannot distinguish between these four models, with arrows pointing in different directions. If there is no temporal precedence, no manipulation, don't use these models, just use regression.

On the exam you have a fresh JASP, so click the blue plus and select Process to add it to the top bar. In the Models tab you pick a Hayes model number (mediation is number 4, moderation number 1) and tell JASP which variable is the predictor and which is the mediator.

chapter: Path coefficients and the effects tables
summary: The path coefficients table lists the a, b and c paths, the pairwise associations between your variables. The direct and indirect effects table splits the total effect, and here the indirect effect is not significant, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis that there is no indirect effect.

There's also the way described in the book, where you build your path model from the bottom up by creating the different pathways yourself. It is a more flexible approach that can better match your theoretical question, so choose your favorite.

A significant association between mediator and outcome, with no significant association between predictor and outcome, leaves not much to mediate. Always do hypothesis testing with your p-value, because confidence intervals are for estimation.

In the applet you can induce a correlation between the two predictor variables, and that starts to mess up your multiple regression results. A very common pattern is a significant effect in the simple model that disappears the moment you add a second, correlated predictor, because the standard error increases.

An association between predictors is about the value of one variable affecting the value of another variable. An interaction effect is about one predictor influencing the effect of another predictor, and you can have either one without the other.

In mediation analysis we model dependence in a causal way, so be sure that your methodology, your experimental manipulation, allows that. We test mediation by looking at the p-value for the indirect effect, a × b.

Moderation analysis is nothing more than looking at interactions between variables, but now with continuous predictors, because in block 3 life is continuous. Mediation is about one variable affecting the value of another variable, while an interaction is about one predictor influencing the effect of the other.

When we add a moderator, it has an arrow pointing at the association between predictor and outcome. One arrow pointing at another arrow indicates that the moderator is influencing the effect of the predictor on the outcome variable.

The regression formula has the main effect of the predictor, the main effect of the moderator, and a last term, the interaction term. For every coefficient we get a hypothesis test of whether it significantly differs from zero, and that is how we test the interaction effect.

With two predictors, the model predictions are shown by a two-dimensional plane. The model with just the two main effects is a flat square, while with an interaction there is a bend in it, and that bend is exactly what an interaction effect tells you.

The assumptions are the same as for linear regression, because process models are basically collections of linear regressions. The Process module has no assumption checks, so on the exam you assess the assumptions using multiple regression.

Our outcome is wakefulness, how awake people are, with two predictors, how long somebody has been awake and how much coffee they have consumed. An interaction would mean that the effect of coffee depends on how long somebody has been awake.

The observed correlations give a first idea of how strongly the variables are correlated, but they do not say anything about interaction effects. A matrix scatter plot is more informative, because we are looking at the raw data and can see, for instance, problems with linear associations.

With a 3D scatter plot, we fit a square into the points in such a way that all the distances are as small as possible. A much better way to visualize two predictors is the descriptives plot in linear regression.

Just as in the ANOVA descriptives plots, you put the second predictor in separate lines, and JASP groups it into, for instance, low, medium and high. If these lines are parallel there is no interaction effect, but we always follow up with a more formal test with a p-value.

We get estimates for the two main effects and the interaction effect, each with a standard error, a t-value and a p-value. For our alpha of 0.005 we reject the null hypothesis for all three coefficients.

Based on the regression coefficients we can predict wakefulness for every participant, for instance someone who was 15 hours awake and drank 213 milliliters of coffee. The values on the predictors are featured twice in this calculation, once for the main effects and once for the interaction effect.

The fitted plane is not a flat surface, there is a curvature to it, and that signals an interaction effect. R-squared is the sum of the blue lines divided by the sum of the orange lines, and here we explain almost 99% of the variance.

What if we didn't measure milliliters of coffee, but cups of coffee instead? Milliliters is the more fine-grained way of measuring coffee consumption, but cups are a lot easier to visualize as separate lines.

In the Process module the Models tab needs a model number, 4 for mediation and 1 for moderation, where the arrow points at the other arrow. The path coefficients table gives the two main effects and the interaction, and with a significant interaction you always interpret the main effects in its context.

By default, JASP shows the conditional effects of your predictor on your outcome for three values of the moderator (the 16th, 50th and 84th percentiles). For the hypothesis test of the interaction, look at the p-value in the third row of the path coefficients table.

In hierarchical regression, model 2 differs from model 1 only by the interaction effect, so we look at the increase in R-squared and its p-value. The R-squared change is sort of the effect size, and a small increase can still be significant for a high enough sample size.

Process centers the predictors by default, which means you subtract the mean, so a main-effect coefficient becomes the effect of that predictor when somebody scores equal to the mean on the other variable. Centering changes the main-effect coefficients, but not the interaction coefficient or its significance.

Process uses the structural equation modeling approach, so it gives a z statistic where linear regression gives a t statistic. They are extremely similar, and on the exam you'll be pointed to the right analysis.

We add the interaction effect as a new model in the Model tab, by Command or Control clicking both predictors. The p-value of the R-squared change and the p-value of the interaction coefficient are the same, because both tell you whether there is a significant interaction effect.

Assess multicollinearity with the VIF of the main-effects-only model, because the VIF will always look problematic in the full model with the interaction. Without the interaction, the residuals versus predicted plot shows a parabola, because there is a strong effect in the data that we are not modeling.

In the applet you can induce multicollinearity and an interaction effect separately. Multicollinearity is about the values of your predictors being associated, while an interaction is about the effect of one variable being influenced by another variable.

chapter: Cups of coffee as a categorical predictor
summary: In regression you can treat cups of coffee as a scale variable (the covariates box) or as a categorical variable (the factors box). Treated as categorical, we throw away information about the order and magnitude of coffee consumption.

We can assess an interaction effect in linear regression, with a hierarchical setup and the assumption checks, or in the Process module, and the interaction coefficient is the same in both. Centering only changes the main-effect coefficients.

The chi-squared test is all about quantifying an association between two categorical variables, the last combination of types of variables. We can do hypothesis testing with a p-value, but we can also look at an effect size, which tells a different story.

We look at what the observed counts are on the one hand, and on the other hand what our null model predicts for these counts. The chi-squared statistic tells you the difference between what you see in the data and what you expect under the null hypothesis, and a big difference is bad news for the null hypothesis.

Like the t- and F-distributions, the chi-squared distribution is shaped by its degrees of freedom, the number of rows minus 1 times the number of columns minus 1. With two categories in each variable, we get a chi-squared distribution with a single degree of freedom.

We want independent observations, where every person only influences their own observation, and the expected counts should not be too small. There is no normality assumption to worry about, because we are only working with categorical variables.

Let's collect some data, with three questions that each have categorical outcomes. Can I predict whether you watch the lectures digitally or live from your self-assessed introversion versus extroversion, and from whether you are a cat, dog, or other animal lover?

With two categorical variables you can display the full data in such a table, without summarizing the data in any way. Is there an association between the two, a difference between the proportion of introverted people and of extroverted people who watch the lectures live?

If personality and lecture style are independent, the probability of somebody being extrovert and watching digitally is the probability of watching digitally times the probability of being extrovert. So we take the row total, multiply it by the column total and divide by n, which gives the expected count for that cell (10.06 extrovert digital viewers).

We take the differences between the observed counts and the counts the null model expects, and a fancy term for these is the residuals. In a two-by-two design they are always flipped, because what we over-predict for one cell we under-predict for the other.
Putting all those numbers into one formula gives a single value, our chi-squared test statistic of 2.38. Is this high or not? We don't really know until we test its significance.

With a single degree of freedom, the probability of observing this chi-squared statistic, or more extreme, is around 12%, which is not significant for our alpha of 0.005. We fail to reject the null hypothesis, so we cannot conclude that there is an association between personality and preferred lecture viewing style.

The regular chi-squared test assumes that the expected cell counts are sufficiently high. In a two-by-two design none should be below 5, and with more groups no more than 20% of the cells should have an expected count below 5.

Just as we could choose the Welch t-test, here you can choose a more robust version, Fisher's exact test, which does not make the assumption about the expected cell counts. Our lowest expected count is 10.06, so we are fine using the regular chi-squared test.

The residuals tell you for which cell in the design the null model is the most wrong, and the standardized residuals make it possible to compare them between cells. A positive or negative sign does not matter, and here the null model was the most wrong for the extrovert digital viewers.

The effect size for categorical associations is a really cool one, but it does take a moment to wrap your head around. A first step is to remember the probability rules that hold when two events are independent.

If A and B are independent, the probability of A given B is simply the probability of A. If personality and viewing style are independent, the probability of preferring the digital lecture if you are an extrovert is the same as the probability of preferring the digital lecture.

The bar chart shows the observed proportions, and the dashed line is the probability of somebody being an extrovert in the sample, 0.44. If the two variables are independent, that probability should be 0.44 among the digital viewers and among the live viewers.

The odds express the counts within one group as a ratio, for instance 1.3 times as many extroverts as introverts among the digital viewers, and 0.58 times as many among the live viewers. If there is an association, we would expect those two odds to be different.
The ratio of those odds is called the odds ratio, and it is the effect size of the chi-squared test. If there is no association the odds ratio is 1, and we observed an odds ratio of 2.25.
We can also look at the odds of digital versus live within the extroverts (0.87) and within the introverts (0.38). The ratio of those odds is still exactly that same odds ratio of 2.25.

We saw two main ways to analyze an association between categorical variables, the chi-squared test with its p-value for hypothesis testing, and the odds ratio as the effect size. JASP by default gives the log of the odds ratio, and because the log of 1 equals 0, the null value of the log odds ratio is 0.

In the Frequencies module, Contingency Tables gives the observed counts and the chi-squared test with its p-value. In the Statistics tab you add the odds ratio (only for two-by-two designs) and Fisher's exact test, and in the Cells tab the expected counts and the Pearson (standardized) residuals.

chapter: A third variable as a layer
summary: Adding a third variable as a layer gives separate contingency tables, and chi-squared tests, for each group of that variable. A significant association for only the dog people would indicate an interaction, but this is more of an exploratory tool than a real test for an interaction effect.

The chi-squared test is the way to assess independent predictors in factorial ANOVA designs, because those predictors are categorical. The balanced design from lecture 17 gives a chi-squared statistic of exactly 0, with a p-value of 1.

The book example is about training cats to dance by offering them food or affection, and it has a fairly strong effect. The chi-squared value of 25.36 has a very low p-value, so we reject the null hypothesis, and in the food group 2.8 times as many cats danced as did not dance.

It's all about quantifying associations between categorical variables, with a hypothesis test (the chi-squared statistic and its p-value) and an effect size (the odds ratio). Effect sizes allow you to interpret your results in a more theoretically interesting way, rather than just saying reject or fail to reject the null.

For the final statistics lecture of SSR, today's topic is Bayesian ANOVA. Throughout the course we got very close to how statistics is being done in the real world, talking about assumptions, interactions and dependence between predictors.

The frequentist framework is all about asking what happens in the long run to my statistical test, in terms of type 1 and type 2 error rates. If you want to do a hypothesis test or parameter estimation, you are not limited to this framework, and the Bayesian framework also allows you to do inferential statistics, with some different metrics.

We repeat the core Bayesian concepts, apply these to ANOVA, and do a Bayesian ANOVA in JASP, which is the analysis that you need to know for the exam. Chapters one through six of the booklet reintroduce the core concepts, and the new chapter for today is chapter 7 about ANOVA.

Many years ago we did a beer tasting test in our lab, where people tasted 2 unmarked cups of beer and had to say which of the two was the alcoholic one. If people cannot taste the difference, they are guessing, and θ, the probability of a correct response, is 0.5.

The Bayesian framework is all based on this continuous updating of knowledge. We start with prior knowledge, derive predictions, test those against the observed data, and use the prediction error to update our knowledge, so what we end up with today is our starting knowledge of tomorrow.

We start with some prior beliefs and update them with the data, and that updating step is completely based on how well every individual value of the parameter predicted the data. Together they form our posterior beliefs, what we have learned after observing the data.

In the Bayesian framework we look at different models, and each model reflects its beliefs about the parameter by a probability distribution. Sarah believes θ is exactly 0.5 and Paul is really sure it is 0.8, and because they go all in on a single value we call these point models.

Based on what a model says about the parameter, we can derive the likely outcomes of an experiment with 10 tasters, which is no different from the sampling distribution. Asking each model how likely our observed 8 out of 10 is (the yellow bar) and taking the ratio of the two yellow bars gives exactly the Bayes factor.

Models can also state multiple values, like Alex's open-minded model, which believes that every value of the proportion correct is equally likely before seeing the data. Any model that makes a statement about the parameter gives a sampling distribution, which shows what outcomes to expect if this model is the true model.

Betty's model puts probability mass on all values between 0.5 and 1 and none on values lower than 0.5, so it claims that people can distinguish between the alcoholic and non-alcoholic beers. Averaging the sampling distributions of all values Betty claims gives the average sampling distribution, and its yellow bar shows how likely 8 out of 10 is under her model.

These statements of the models are prior distributions, and prior distributions are always probability distributions. A prior for a proportion needs the domain zero to one, and one convenient distribution that follows those criteria is the beta distribution.
Let's say we observe 8 successes out of 10. To update the prior distributions with this data, we look at the likelihood of the observed data for every value in the model.

The likelihood function is not a probability distribution, it maps every value of θ onto the likelihood of the observed data, around 0.3 for θ = 0.8. It is always the same, whichever model you are updating, because it only depends on the type of data, here the binomial likelihood.

The marginal likelihood is the average likelihood of the observed data for all values in the model, so unlike the likelihood it depends on the model. For Alex's model it is around 0.09, and it quite literally sets the bar for what we consider better than average predictions.

The likelihood divided by the marginal likelihood is the predictive updating factor, which is greater than one exactly when that value of the parameter predicted the data better than average. Those values see a boost in plausibility, and values of 0.55 and lower and 0.95 and higher, which predicted the data worse than average, suffer a penalty.

Compared to Alex's prior distribution, the posterior density has increased for all values that had a higher than average likelihood. Models with a single value, like Sarah's, don't learn from the data, because no amount of data is going to change their beliefs.

A point estimate such as the posterior median is our best guess, but an interval estimate also reflects uncertainty, and the Bayesian version is the credible interval. If Alex's model is the true model, there is a 95% probability that the true value of the proportion is between 0.48 and 0.94.

The marginal likelihood for Alex's model, 0.09, is exactly the height of the yellow bar in Alex's sampling distribution, how likely 8 out of 10 is on average under that model. It differs for the different models (around 0.17 for Betty), and we use exactly those numbers to do model comparison.

Hypothesis testing compares different models to each other, and null and alternative are really just labels. It is more important to pay attention to how you translate your research question into a statistical statement, such as θ = 0.5 if people cannot taste the difference between the beers.

In the same way that we update beliefs about parameter values, we can update beliefs about which of two models did a better job in predicting the data. The prior odds tell you how many times more likely one model is than the other before seeing the data, and updating them with the data gives the posterior odds.

The updating factor from prior odds to posterior odds is the Bayes factor, the ratio of the marginal likelihoods of two models. A BF10 of 3 means that the data are three times more likely under the alternative hypothesis than under the null hypothesis, and a BF01 flips that interpretation, so always report the subscript.

The marginal likelihood of 8 out of 10 is 0.04 under Sarah's model and 0.09 under Alex's model. Their ratio, the Bayes factor comparing Sarah to Alex, is 0.48, which means the data are about twice as likely (2.07 times) under Alex's model as under Sarah's model.

There exist certain words you can associate with values of the Bayes factor, for instance a Bayes factor between 1 and 3 is anecdotal evidence. You don't need to memorize these labels, but you do need to know the definition of the Bayes factor, and an exam question that asks for a decision will tell you which Bayes factor threshold to use.

In JASP we represent Bayes factors with pizza plots, where the proportion of mozzarella and tomato sauce shows the evidence for each of the two hypotheses. A Bayes factor of 1 means the data are as likely under both models, and we can even get evidence in favor of the null hypothesis, which is not possible with p-values.

The Bayes factor assesses a model's performance in a continuous way, you can look at the data as you are gathering it and stop when you have decisive evidence, and it distinguishes evidence of absence from absence of evidence. A Bayes factor of 1.5, for instance, is not very decisive, which means the data are not informative enough to decide between the two models.

ANOVA is just a regression, also in Bayesian ANOVA, so we still represent the model with dummy variables. The regression slope b1 indicates the group difference between our two groups, and if b1 equals 0, there is no difference between the groups.

The null model states that the regression coefficient is 0, a single spike at 0, while the alternative model puts a Cauchy distribution on it, with most mass around 0 but also quite some mass on other values. In the Bayesian framework we need to make explicit what the alternative predicts, more than just the direction, by choosing its prior distribution.

chapter: Marginal likelihoods and the Bayes factor
summary: For both models we can ask how well they predicted the data on average, and the data are very unlikely under the null model that states the coefficient equals 0. The ratio of the two marginal likelihoods, the Bayes factor, is around 10,000, so the data are 10,000 times more likely under the alternative model than under the null model.

The Bayesian ANOVA sits under ANOVA in JASP, and here we predict people's confidence rating from whether they correctly identified the alcoholic beer. By default, the BF10 column compares every model to the best model at the top, and the inclusion Bayes factor (here 1.3) compares the models with a predictor to the models without it.

With a second predictor, whether people tasted the alcoholic beer first, JASP lists five models, up to the full model with both main effects and their interaction. The two main outputs to focus on for the exam are the BF10 column in the model comparison table and the inclusion Bayes factor from the effects table.

Bayesian statistics is still a thing, and you can do Bayesian versions of all the analyses we've seen in SSR. I would like you to primarily understand the Bayesian ANOVA, which is explained in the booklet.

chapter: Bayes and open science in the wild
summary: A large-scale investigation of the psychology literature over the past 20 years shows a nice increase in how many articles use Bayesian statistics. Open data, preregistration and reporting the statistical software have also improved, making for a little more robust science.

Our central SSR formula, outcome equals model plus error, holds three things we are now getting a grip on. Statistics is a very relative endeavor, the assumptions are a very important part of robust statistics, and complete reporting means a number for accuracy and graphs for some vibes.

Different metrics answer different research questions, such as whether we have evidence for an effect (a p-value or a Bayes factor) or which model predicted the best. Multiverse analysis, which is not part of the exam, helps you get a grip on sometimes arbitrary choices.
The exam notes from the previous lectures of block 3 are at the end of the slides. Thank you for all your energy, I wish you all the best in your future studies, and see you next week at the exam.
